title: Things That Help: Weekly Wrap-Up Video for Parents
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. shares and analyzes a practice from a veteran colleague, 32-year English teacher Ed McCarthy, who records a single weekly screencast wrap-up video for parents summarizing what happened in class. Stuart breaks down why the tactic works using his own CCP (Care, Competence, Passion) credibility framework, arguing that the video lets parents infer Ed's competence and care themselves rather than being told about it, which parents then reinforce back to their own children at home. He highlights that the video replaces vague parent-teacher conversations with specific shared vocabulary, sentence length, Learning Partners, particular assignments, which he says multiplies the effect of classroom lessons and heads off the adversarial dynamic that can develop between teachers and families. Crucially, Stuart frames this as a workload win rather than an add-on: the video repurposes lesson-planning content Ed is already creating rather than generating new work, which he holds up as the model for high-leverage teacher communication generally.
points: The featured teacher, 'Ed' McCarthy, sends a single weekly screencast recapping class content to parents; Stuart frames this as simultaneously boosting teacher credibility, instructional clarity, and the home-school relationship in under five minutes of parent time.

Stuart applies his CCP framework (Care, Competence, Passion) to explain why the video works: it lets parents infer credibility themselves rather than being told, which then gets reinforced back to the student by the parent.

The workload case is explicit: the video doesn't create new work because it repurposes lesson-planning content Ed already produces; Stuart holds this up as the model for high-leverage teacher communication generally.
By giving parents specific vocabulary instead of vague class-content talk, the video is credited with preventing the adversarial parent-teacher dynamic that Stuart says is otherwise common.
quotes: This isn't something I've done for my students' families but, gosh, does it seem like a simple method for radically increasing teacher clarity, teacher credibility, and the home-school partnership.
Ed's polish and poise is the fruit of hard-won expertise. He's been teaching English for 32 years and has coached 80 seasons (!) of football, wrestling, and lacrosse.

Mr. MC has made it easy to believe that their child is in the class of a credible teacher — someone who cares, is competent, and is passionate. Ed is nailing CCP, and when you do that with parents, you end up having parents reinforcing your credibility with their children.

This weekend, the parent/guardians of Mr. MC's students won't need to have vague conversations about what's happening in their English class — they'll be able to talk about sentence length, or home-writing, or what it means to be a better student.
Too often, the relationship between teachers and parents/guardians becomes borderline adversarial. I'm sure that Ed experiences this sometimes, but with messaging like this it's got to be rare.

Perhaps best of all, from a teacher workload perspective Ed hasn't created a monster here. He's taking lesson planning pieces that he already needs to create, and he's sharing them via screencast with parents.
